sentences.text: The known fossil skeleton measured 14.3 cm from the nose to the 17th tail bone, while the total body length is estimated at about 20 cm.
Its head featured a broad, flat shape with eyes set far forward and a snout shorter than the back part of the skull.
The nostrils were tiny, measuring only 1.5 mm in length and shaped almost like a square or trapezoid.
A large eye socket with a 6 mm diameter lacked the ring-like bones often found in aquatic reptiles.
The openings on the top of the skull were small, with a length of just 4.5 mm.
The skeleton contains 20 neck vertebrae, 19 back vertebrae, 3 hip vertebrae, and at least 17 tail vertebrae.
Back vertebrae lacked long side projections but possessed very thick joint surfaces.
Ribs along the back were single-headed, unusually long, and heavily thickened.
The upper arm bone was 10 mm long with uneven muscle attachments, while the forearm bones were each 5 mm long and equal in width.
The thigh bone was 14 mm long, slender, slightly curved, and bore distinct lines on both ends.
The shin bone was slightly longer than the main lower leg bone, measuring 6.5 mm compared to 6 mm.
Despite its tiny size of roughly 20 cm, this creature possessed a surprisingly robust build.
The genus was first named by a research team including Jun Liu and Olivier Rieppel in 2011.
It lived during the lower Middle Triassic, specifically the Anisian age, in Yunnan Province, southwestern China.
Fossils were found in the Middle Triassic Guanling Formation Lagerstätte.
Scientists hypothesize that pachypleurosaurs originated in the eastern Tethys Ocean before spreading to the western Tethys.
Dianopachysaurus is classified within the superorder Sauropterygia, order Nothosauroidea, suborder Pachypleurosauria, and family Keichousauridae.
The type species is Dianopachysaurus dingi, described by Liu et al. in 2011.
It belongs to the family Keichousauridae.
